paragraphs: For a minute or two she stood looking at the house, wondering what to do next, when suddenly a footman in uniform came running out of the woods. (She decided he was a footman because he was wearing a uniform. Judging by his face alone, she would have called him a fish.) He rapped loudly on the door with his knuckles. It was opened by another footman in uniform, with a round face and large eyes like a frog’s. Both footmen, Alice noticed, had powdered hair that curled all over their heads. She was very curious to know what it was all about, and she crept a little way out of the woods to listen.

The Fish-Footman began by pulling a great letter from under his arm, nearly as big as himself, and handed it to the other, saying in a solemn voice, “For the Duchess. An invitation from the Queen to play croquet.” The Frog-Footman repeated, in the same solemn tone, only changing the order of the words a little, “From the Queen. An invitation for the Duchess to play croquet.”
Then they both bowed low, and their curls got tangled together.

Alice laughed so hard at this that she had to run back into the woods for fear they would hear her. When she next peeped out, the Fish-Footman was gone, and the other was sitting on the ground near the door, staring stupidly up at the sky.
Alice went timidly up to the door and knocked.

“There’s no point in knocking,” said the Footman, “and for two reasons. First, because I’m on the same side of the door as you are. Second, because they’re making such a racket inside that no one could possibly hear you.” And there was certainly an extraordinary noise going on inside, a constant howling and sneezing, and every now and then a great crash, as if a dish or kettle had been smashed to pieces.
“Then please,” said Alice, “how am I supposed to get in?”

“There might be some sense in your knocking,” the Footman went on without paying attention to her, “if we had the door between us. For instance, if you were inside, you could knock, and I could let you out, you know.” He was looking up at the sky the whole time he was speaking, which Alice thought was decidedly rude. “But maybe he can’t help it,” she said to herself. “His eyes are so very nearly at the top of his head. But still, he could answer questions. How am I supposed to get in?” she repeated aloud.
“I shall sit here,” the Footman remarked, “until tomorrow—”
At that moment the door of the house opened, and a large plate came skimming out, straight at the Footman’s head. It just grazed his nose and smashed to pieces against one of the trees behind him.
“—or the next day, maybe,” the Footman continued in the same tone, exactly as if nothing had happened.
“How am I supposed to get in?” asked Alice again, in a louder voice.
“Are you supposed to get in at all?” said the Footman. “That’s the first question, you know.”
It was, no doubt, but Alice didn’t like being told so. “It’s really dreadful,” she muttered to herself, “the way all these creatures argue. It’s enough to drive a person crazy!”
The Footman seemed to think this was a good chance to repeat his remark with variations. “I shall sit here,” he said, “on and off, for days and days.”
“But what am I supposed to do?” said Alice.
“Anything you like,” said the Footman, and he began whistling.
“Oh, there’s no use talking to him,” said Alice desperately. “He’s completely idiotic!” And she opened the door and went in.

The door led straight into a large kitchen, which was full of smoke from one end to the other. The Duchess was sitting on a three-legged stool in the middle, nursing a baby. The cook was leaning over the fire, stirring a large cauldron that seemed to be full of soup.
“There’s definitely too much pepper in that soup!” Alice said to herself, as well as she could between sneezes.

There was definitely too much of it in the air. Even the Duchess sneezed now and then, and as for the baby, it was alternately sneezing and howling without a moment’s pause. The only things in the kitchen that weren’t sneezing were the cook and a large cat sitting on the hearth, grinning from ear to ear.
“Could you please tell me,” said Alice, a little timidly, because she wasn’t quite sure it was good manners for her to speak first, “why your cat grins like that?”
“It’s a Cheshire cat,” said the Duchess, “and that’s why. Pig!”
She said the last word with such sudden violence that Alice jumped. But she saw a moment later that it was meant for the baby and not for her, so she took courage and went on:
“I didn’t know Cheshire cats always grinned. In fact, I didn’t know cats could grin.”
“They all can,” said the Duchess, “and most of them do.”
“I don’t know of any that do,” Alice said very politely, feeling quite pleased to have gotten into a conversation.
“You don’t know much,” said the Duchess, “and that’s a fact.”

Alice didn’t like the tone of this remark at all and thought it would be a good idea to bring up some other subject. While she was trying to think of one, the cook took the cauldron of soup off the fire and immediately began throwing everything within reach at the Duchess and the baby. The fire tools came first, followed by a shower of saucepans, plates, and dishes. The Duchess took no notice of them even when they hit her, and the baby was already howling so much that it was impossible to tell whether the blows hurt it or not.

“Oh, please watch what you’re doing!” cried Alice, jumping up and down in an agony of fear. “Oh, there goes his precious nose!” as an unusually large saucepan flew close by it and very nearly took it off.
“If everybody minded their own business,” the Duchess said in a hoarse growl, “the world would go around a lot faster than it does.”

“Which would not be an advantage,” said Alice, who was very glad of a chance to show off a little of her knowledge. “Just think what a mess it would make of day and night! You see, the earth takes twenty-four hours to turn around on its axis—”
“Speaking of axes,” said the Duchess, “chop off her head!”

Alice glanced rather anxiously at the cook to see if she meant to take the hint, but the cook was busily stirring the soup and didn’t seem to be listening, so she went on: “Twenty-four hours, I think. Or is it twelve? I—”

“Oh, don’t bother me,” said the Duchess. “I never could stand numbers!” And with that she began nursing her child again, singing a sort of lullaby to it as she did so and giving it a violent shake at the end of every line:
“Speak roughly to your little boy, And beat him when he sneezes: He only does it to annoy, Because he knows it teases.”
CHORUS. (In which the cook and the baby joined):
“Wow! wow! wow!”
While the Duchess sang the second verse of the song, she kept tossing the baby violently up and down, and the poor little thing howled so loudly that Alice could hardly hear the words:
“I speak severely to my boy, I beat him when he sneezes; For he can thoroughly enjoy The pepper when he pleases!”
CHORUS.
“Wow! wow! wow!”

“Here! You can nurse it a bit if you like!” the Duchess said to Alice, flinging the baby at her as she spoke. “I have to go and get ready to play croquet with the Queen,” and she hurried out of the room. The cook threw a frying pan after her as she went, but it just missed her.

Alice caught the baby with some difficulty, because it was an oddly shaped little creature that held out its arms and legs in all directions, “just like a starfish,” thought Alice. The poor little thing was snorting like a steam engine when she caught it, and it kept curling itself up and straightening out again, so that for the first minute or two it was all she could do to hold on to it.

As soon as she had figured out the proper way to hold it (which was to twist it into a sort of knot and then keep a tight grip on its right ear and left foot so it couldn’t undo itself), she carried it out into the open air. “If I don’t take this child with me,” thought Alice, “they’re sure to kill it in a day or two. Wouldn’t it be murder to leave it behind?” She said the last words out loud, and the little thing grunted in reply (it had stopped sneezing by this time). “Don’t grunt,” said Alice. “That’s not a proper way to express yourself.”

The baby grunted again, and Alice looked anxiously into its face to see what was wrong. There was no doubt that it had a very turned-up nose, much more like a snout than a real nose. Its eyes, too, were getting extremely small for a baby. Altogether Alice didn’t like the look of the thing at all. “But maybe it was only sobbing,” she thought, and she looked into its eyes again to see if there were any tears.

No, there were no tears. “If you’re going to turn into a pig, my dear,” said Alice seriously, “I’ll have nothing more to do with you. Mind now!” The poor little thing sobbed again (or grunted, it was impossible to say which), and they went on for a while in silence.

Alice was just beginning to think to herself, “Now what am I going to do with this creature when I get it home?” when it grunted again, so violently that she looked down into its face in alarm. This time there was no mistake: it was neither more nor less than a pig, and she felt it would be absurd to carry it any farther.

So she set the little creature down and felt quite relieved to see it trot away quietly into the woods. “If it had grown up,” she said to herself, “it would have been a terribly ugly child. But it makes a rather handsome pig, I think.” And she began thinking of other children she knew who might do very well as pigs, and was just saying to herself, “If only one knew the right way to change them—” when she was a little startled to see the Cheshire Cat sitting on a branch of a tree a few yards away.
The Cat only grinned when it saw Alice. It looked good-natured, she thought. Still, it had very long claws and a great many teeth, so she felt it ought to be treated with respect.

“Cheshire Puss,” she began rather timidly, since she had no idea whether it would like the name. However, it only grinned a little wider. “Well, it’s pleased so far,” thought Alice, and she went on. “Would you please tell me which way I ought to go from here?”
“That depends a good deal on where you want to get to,” said the Cat.
“I don’t much care where,” said Alice.
“Then it doesn’t matter which way you go,” said the Cat.
“As long as I get somewhere,” Alice added as an explanation.
“Oh, you’re sure to do that,” said the Cat, “if you only walk long enough.”
Alice felt this couldn’t be denied, so she tried another question. “What sort of people live around here?”
“In that direction,” the Cat said, waving its right paw around, “lives a Hatter. And in that direction,” waving the other paw, “lives a March Hare. Visit either one you like. They’re both mad.”
“But I don’t want to go among mad people,” Alice remarked.
“Oh, you can’t help that,” said the Cat. “We’re all mad here. I’m mad. You’re mad.”
“How do you know I’m mad?” said Alice.
“You must be,” said the Cat, “or you wouldn’t have come here.”
Alice didn’t think that proved anything, but she went on, “And how do you know you’re mad?”
“To begin with,” said the Cat, “a dog’s not mad. Do you agree?”
“I suppose so,” said Alice.
“Well, then,” the Cat went on, “a dog growls when it’s angry and wags its tail when it’s pleased. Now, I growl when I’m pleased and wag my tail when I’m angry. Therefore I’m mad.”
“I call it purring, not growling,” said Alice.
“Call it what you like,” said the Cat. “Are you playing croquet with the Queen today?”
“I’d like to very much,” said Alice, “but I haven’t been invited yet.”
“You’ll see me there,” said the Cat, and vanished.
Alice wasn’t very surprised at this, because she was getting so used to strange things happening. While she was looking at the spot where it had been, it suddenly appeared again.
“By the way, what happened to the baby?” said the Cat. “I almost forgot to ask.”
“It turned into a pig,” Alice answered calmly, as if the Cat had come back in the most natural way.
“I thought it would,” said the Cat, and vanished again.

Alice waited a little, half expecting to see it again, but it didn’t appear, and after a minute or two she walked on in the direction where the March Hare was said to live. “I’ve seen hatters before,” she said to herself. “The March Hare will be much more interesting, and since it’s May, maybe it won’t be raving mad. At least not as mad as it was in March.” As she said this, she looked up, and there was the Cat again, sitting on a branch of a tree.
“Did you say pig, or fig?” said the Cat.
“I said pig,” replied Alice. “And I wish you wouldn’t keep appearing and vanishing so suddenly. You make me quite dizzy.”
“All right,” said the Cat, and this time it vanished very slowly, beginning with the tip of its tail and ending with the grin, which stayed behind for some time after the rest of it had gone.
“Well! I’ve often seen a cat without a grin,” thought Alice, “but a grin without a cat! That’s the most curious thing I’ve ever seen in my life!”

She hadn’t gone much farther when she came in sight of the March Hare’s house. She thought it must be the right place, because the chimneys were shaped like ears and the roof was thatched with fur. It was such a large house that she didn’t want to go nearer until she had nibbled some more of the left-hand piece of mushroom and raised herself to about two feet tall. Even then she walked up toward it rather timidly, saying to herself, “What if it turns out to be raving mad after all? I almost wish I’d gone to see the Hatter instead!”
